criteria.descriptor: Correctly explains why accuracy misleads under a 1% base rate (trivial-baseline / accuracy paradox) and correctly characterizes the recommended metrics — precision vs recall defined the right way round, F-beta/PR-AUC used appropriately. No incorrect claims such as recommending plain accuracy, swapping precision and recall, or asserting ROC-AUC is the best imbalance metric without qualification.

Covers all key elements: the imbalance/trivial-baseline problem, the move to class-specific precision and recall, the recall emphasis driven by the false-negative cost, and an imbalance-appropriate summary or curve (PR-AUC / F-beta) plus threshold or baseline comparison. Full marks require both the diagnosis and a concrete metric recommendation.

Explicitly ties the metric choice to the 1% base rate and to the false-negative-worse-than-false-positive cost asymmetry, rather than merely listing metric names. Full marks explain WHY recall (or F-beta with beta>1) follows from the cost structure.
Clear, well-organized, review-appropriate explanation that uses metric terminology correctly and would let a non-expert stakeholder understand why 99% accuracy should not decide the ship call.

expected_answer_points: Explains the accuracy paradox: at a 1% base rate a trivial 'always predict not-fraud' classifier already achieves ~99% accuracy while catching no fraud, so the figure carries no evidence of skill.
Notes that accuracy weights all transactions equally, so the majority (legitimate) class dominates and the rare positive class is effectively invisible.
Recommends inspecting the confusion matrix and reporting class-specific precision and recall for the fraud (positive) class rather than a single aggregate number.
Prioritizes recall/sensitivity on the fraud class because false negatives (missed fraud) are the costly error, and justifies this with the stated cost asymmetry.
Recommends a curve/summary suited to imbalance — precision-recall curve or PR-AUC, and/or an F-beta with beta>1 (e.g. F2) — and notes PR-AUC is more informative than ROC-AUC under heavy imbalance.
Connects the final metric/threshold choice to the business cost trade-off (e.g. selecting a threshold, reporting precision at a target recall) and comparing against the trivial baseline.
common_pitfalls: Names F1 as the fix but treats precision and recall as equally important, ignoring that the stated cost asymmetry calls for weighting recall (F-beta with beta>1 / F2), not plain F1.

Recommends ROC-AUC as the primary metric without noting it can look deceptively strong under extreme imbalance because the large true-negative count inflates it; PR-AUC is more sensitive to performance on the rare class.
Confuses precision (of flagged transactions, how many are truly fraud) with recall (of actual frauds, how many were caught), reversing which one the cost asymmetry favors.
Claims accuracy is fine as long as the held-out set is large enough, missing that the problem is the base rate, not sample size.
Dodges the metric question by answering with data-level fixes ('collect more fraud examples', 'oversample/SMOTE', 'rebalance the classes') instead of proposing an evaluation metric.
Lists metrics without connecting the choice back to the business cost, so the recommendation reads as a checklist rather than a justified decision.
reference_answer:
Accuracy is untrustworthy here because of the extreme class imbalance. With a 1% fraud rate, a trivial model that predicts 'not fraud' for every transaction already scores 99% accuracy while catching zero frauds. So 99% is indistinguishable from the do-nothing baseline and says nothing about the model's ability to find the rare positive class. Accuracy weights every transaction equally, so the 99% of legitimate cases dominate the number and the fraud class is effectively invisible.

Instead I would look at the confusion matrix and report class-specific metrics for the fraud (positive) class: precision (of the transactions we flag, how many are truly fraud) and recall/sensitivity (of the actual frauds, how many we catch). Because a false negative is far costlier than a false positive, recall on the fraud class is the priority — we want to catch as much fraud as possible even at the cost of extra manual reviews. To summarize the trade-off I'd use an F-beta score with beta > 1 (e.g. F2) to weight recall over precision, and evaluate the precision-recall curve / PR-AUC rather than ROC-AUC, since PR curves are far more informative than ROC under heavy imbalance (the huge true-negative count inflates ROC-AUC). Finally I'd choose the operating threshold from the cost trade-off — e.g. report precision at a target recall — and always compare against the trivial baseline, not just quote accuracy.
